articles.body: James’ FPL Strategy: Chips Early, Regrets Later - Full90 FPL Skip to content James’ FPL Strategy: Chips Early, Regrets Later In this piece, I (James) will cover my final thoughts for the start of the Fantasy Premier League (FPL) season. I will set out my strategy, reveal my watchlist and show you my two drafts I am picking between ahead of the first deadline on Friday. Let’s get into it. Chips I think the place to start is with chips, because they’re gonna dictate everything about the initial setup. Without chips, I’d build differently. But with them, the plan is pretty clear. Bench Boost Triple Captain Free Hit Wildcard GW1 or 2 GW3 – Haaland v.s Coventry GW 4 or ignore it for later GW4-7 I’m going to bench boost in game week one or two. Just to get rid of it. I don’t even mind if it’s just six points. I don’t think it matters that much. So if I’m fine with a small return, then I might as well go bold with it. Meaning a chase for a defensive triple-up or double up. And, because I don’t think it matters much and I don’t want to spend big, that basically means choosing between Ipswich at home to Sunderland in game week one or Coventry at home to Hull in game week two. I’m leaning one way, but I’m not locked in yet. I’m also very likely to triple captain Haaland in game week three against Coventry. It’s early, he’s fit, no European rotation yet, and historically, he starts fast. I’d rather bank that than wait months for the fixture against Hull that he might not play. Wildcard? I think that’s an early play too. Somewhere between game weeks four and seven. There’s just too many unknowns right now. I’m not fully confident on a lot of things this season given how much change there has been in the league. I also don’t know who the cheap defcon defenders are, or whether defcon is going to matter as much this year. I don’t know which six million forwards will get decent minutes. And, I don’t know whether the more expensive mids (like Saka or Palmer) are worth it. A few weeks of real football answers a lot of those questions. We learn so much early on and I want to use that information to beat my mates. I also like the idea of using the free hit early too, possibly game week four, because there are mini fixture swings across the opening six weeks. And if I don’t wildcard then, the free hit lets me maximize one of them – Chelsea, Palace and Brighton play the promoted teams. Coincidentally, it also lets me own JP in the best fixture after I shit on him so much. Strategy: Be Aggressive Last season I used all my chips in the first seven weeks and it worked well. So same mindset now. The lack of information that we have right now means that the AI models and everyone else’s judgement is at its weakest. I want to try to exploit that. Target the promoted sides, especially Hull. Those are the only fixtures I’m genuinely confident about. Beyond that, I think the middle of the league is tightly packed like last year . It’s not always clear who’s good or bad yet. So I’m going hard when it comes to targeting those promoted teams, but otherwise, I’d rather trust good players than overreact to fixtures. Fixtures mattered less last season, and I suspect that’ll continue. James’ Watchlist I am not fully set on my 15 but I know I am picking from this lot. Goalkeepers Donnarumma – 5.5 Kinsky – 4.5 Verbruggen – 4.5 Rushworth – 4.5 In goal, the decision is whether to go cheap or to get the cheapest, most nailed route into the City defence. Defenders Virgil – 6.5 Tarkowski – 6.0 One of Mosquera, White, Calafiori – 5.5 Maguire – 5.0 Shaw – 4.5 Diop – 4.0 O’Shea – 4.0 Thomas – 4.0 van Ewijk – 4.0 In defence, I LOVE the defcon output of Tarko over multiple seasons and he has been in almost all my tinkers. Then it is a question of whether to take a bit of a risk on whether any of these Arsenal guys will be nailed in a few weeks time or just pay up for the safety of Virgil’s starts in a worse defence. Alongside them I will almost certainly have Shaw but I have tinkered with Maguire in the Virgil or Tarko slot – I can just see the upside with big slabhead getting a goal and defcons in the opening two. And then it’s the promoted shitters. Midfielders B. Fernandes – 12.0 Mbeumo – 8.0 Wirtz – 7.5 Szoboszlai – 7.0 Dango – 6.5 Anderson – 6.5 Schade – 6.0 Ampadu – 5.5 Slater – 4.5 In midfield, I flirted with no Bruno and having Isak instead at the start of the season but Joe turned me around on that one (ironic when you see his team…). Dango has been in almost all my tinkers because I think people are really overlooking him. Szobo has likewise been in all my tinkers because of his routes to points I’ve toyed with Wirtz or Mbeumo in the 4th slot but I am leaning Mbeumo because of the opening two and then just moving off him in 3 if I want to. In the 5th slot, I am pretty settled on Anderson after the compelling case made by Joe. I have toyed with Schade there because I think he is also underrated. Ampadu I like as a defcon guy but I am not sure that I feel confident to start him every week and don’t like paying 5.5 for him to sit on my bench. Slater is just the only nailed 4.5 I think I know. Forwards Haaland – 15.5 Joao Pedro – 7.5 Calvert-Lewin – 6.0 McBurnie – 5.5 Walle Egeli – 4.5 Up top, Haaland hasn’t left a single tinker and neither has Calvert-Lewin… but for different reasons. Haaland is a perma cap option and always starts the season hot. DCL is nailed for me because he’s the only 6.0 I trust to play 90s consistently. JP and I have a complicated history but I don’t actually rate him that much and think he is only good against bad teams. But, alongside being contrarian and arrogant, I am also a coward that fears his 60% ownership so he makes this list. McBurnie would be my hedge if I bench boosted in 2 in case Hull scored my money would be on him. And Walle Egeli is my bench boost 1 striker because he’s dirt cheap and I don’t care if he doesn’t play… James’ Draft Or How I Learned To Stop Worrying About 4.5 Forwards I pretty famously (lol) came out heavily in favour of bench boost 2 and triple Coventry defence. The logic is still sound. If you, like me, don’t care about doing okay on bench boost (10-12 points) then you should risk it all for big bench boost (20 points) or a shit one (6 points) by getting a triple Coventry defence – something like Rushworth, Thomas and van Ewijk. It looks like this: I’ve got some great picks with some great fixtures in there but 5.5 McBurnie on my bench just doesn’t sit well with me. Enter Walle. I don’t know who he is but he’s had a good pre-season and he looks to be starting gameweek 1 and look at what I can do with that extra 1.0: I’ve upgraded Maguire to Tarko. Got Mbeumo over Wirtz for the first two. And I have the basic bitch goalkeeper rotation of Kinsky and Verbruggen. And all it cost me was McBurnie to Walle. And my dignity. And reputation. Fortunately for me, not many people read this website but you can change that, tell your friends! (never miss an opportunity for a shameless plug). So, that’s my current draft and basically my dilemma. Whichever one I go for will probably be wrong. And, I have cursed myself by tinkering in and out every player in the game so when anyone scores in gameweek 1 I can say: ‘I had him in one of my drafts.’ Such is life. Such is FPL. articles.title: The FPL Team Planner That Does Your Homework For You: Import, Project, Optimise
articles.excerpt: Every FPL manager runs the same loop: check fixtures, second-guess transfers, wonder if the armband is right. The Statz Team Planner runs that loop for you - import your real squad in seconds, see projected points on every player for the next six gameweeks, and let the optimiser propose transfer plans with the reasoning attached. Here's everything it does.

articles.body: FPL Team Planner - Import Your Squad & Optimise Transfers The FPL Team Planner That Does Your Homework For You: Import, Project, Optimise Every FPL manager runs the same weekly loop. Check the fixtures. Second-guess two transfers. Wonder whether the captaincy is right. Do it all in your head, on a bus, four minutes before the deadline. The Statz FPL Team Planner exists to run that loop properly: your actual squad, projected points on every player, fixtures for the run ahead, and an optimiser that proposes your next moves - with its reasoning shown. It's the piece of the Statz FPL toolkit that ties everything else together, and this is the full tour: what it does, how the optimiser thinks, and why the managers using it are making decisions with numbers the official app simply doesn't have. Get your squad in, in seconds Three ways in, no typing your team out player by player. Enter your FPL Team ID and the planner pulls your real squad, bank and chips. Start from scratch if you're planning a draft. Or - the party trick - upload a screenshot of your team from the official app, and the planner reads the players off the image and rebuilds your squad automatically. Once you're in, your squad, transfers and plans save to your account, so the plan you sketch on your laptop is waiting on your phone at the deadline. The pitch view: your team, with the numbers switched on The planner's home screen looks like your team - a proper pitch, shirts, bench - but every player carries the number the official app never shows: projected points for the gameweek , from the same Statz model behind the Season Rankings . The header runs the totals for you: your bank, free transfers, a Team Rating out of 100 , and your squad's total projected points for the gameweek. The pitch view: projected points on every shirt, captaincy marked, and your gameweek total in the header. Step forward through the gameweeks with the arrows and the whole squad re-projects against each week's fixtures - so "should I hold this transfer?" becomes a question you can answer by looking. Chips live in the header too, so a Wildcard or Bench Boost can be planned into a specific week rather than panic-played. And the camera button exports your squad as a shareable image for the group chat. The transfer market, sorted by what actually matters The Players panel is a transfer shortlist with projections built in: search anyone, filter by position, club or price, and sort by projected points over the next six gameweeks rather than last season's totals. One column tells you what a player is likely to do for the week ahead; the six-gameweek column tells you what he's worth across the run - which is the number transfers should actually be bought on. The player market, sorted by six-gameweek projected points - the number a transfer should be judged on. Fixtures as a heatmap, three ways The Fixtures tab turns the run-in into a heatmap you can read at a glance, with a gameweek range slider and three modes: projected goals per fixture, clean sheet percentage , and classic FPL FDR if you want the official difficulty view. Totals rank every club across your chosen window, so "whose fixtures turn?" stops being folklore and becomes a sorted column. The fixtures heatmap in projected-goals mode: every club's run, quantified and ranked over your chosen gameweeks. Optimise: the feature that earns the bookmark Then there's the button that separates this from every fixture ticker and rate-my-team thread: Optimise . It works in two modes. Starting fresh - or holding a wildcard - it builds the best £100m squad for the next six gameweeks outright, with its projected total attached, and loads it straight onto your pitch to tweak. With your real squad in, it proposes a concrete transfer plan instead: which players out, which in, in which gameweek, whether a points hit is worth taking, and what the whole package is projected to gain. Draft mode: the optimiser's best £100m squad for the opening six gameweeks, projected total attached, one tap to load. Two things make it trustworthy rather than a black box. First, every move shows its working : the incoming and outgoing player's projected points for each of the next six fixtures, side by side, with captaincy-ceiling weeks flagged. Second, the "Why these moves?" panel says it in plain English - a fixture swing, a captaincy upgrade, value released from the bank - and the arithmetic is printed at the bottom: points in, points out, minus any hit, equals the net gain. Agree with it and one tap applies the plan; disagree and you've still learned exactly where the model thinks your squad is leaking points. Plans, leagues and the weekly routine Everything you sketch saves as a Plan - so you can keep a safe route and an aggressive route side by side and decide on deadline day, with an undo button for every experiment along the way. The Leagues tab brings your mini-league into the planner, because half of FPL is knowing what the manager above you is likely to do next. Under the hood it's the same engine as the rest of the toolkit: projections built on expected minutes first (the Season Rankings model), refreshed as new data lands, sharpened by the predicted line-ups behind Team News . The planner is where those numbers stop being a leaderboard and start being your decisions: fifteen minutes a week, squad in front of you, projections on every option. The planner is free to try with your own squad at statz.ai/fpl/my-team - full projections and the optimiser are part of FPL Pro FAQs What is the Statz FPL Team Planner? A squad-planning tool at statz.ai/fpl/my-team that loads your real FPL team and adds what the official app doesn't have: projected points on every player, multi-gameweek fixture heatmaps, chip planning, saved transfer plans and an optimiser that proposes your next moves with the reasoning shown. How do I import my FPL team into the planner? Three ways: enter your FPL Team ID and it pulls your squad automatically, build a squad from scratch, or upload a screenshot of your team from the official app and the planner reads your players off the image. What does the FPL optimiser do? It analyses your squad, bank, free transfers and the projections for the coming gameweeks, then proposes specific transfers - including when a points hit is worth it - showing the six-gameweek projection for every player in and out, plus a plain-English explanation and the net expected points gain. Is the FPL Team Planner free? Importing and building your squad is free with a Statz account. Full player projections and the optimiser are part of FPL Pro. articles.body: Why Fixture Difficulty Should be Focused on More for the New Football Season - Premier Fantasy Tools Last updated on August 19th, 2026 Fixture difficulty is one of the most talked about concepts in FPL, and one of the most consistently ignored in football betting. A simple comparison number for some, but those who take it seriously see a far deeper number, weighing up a lot of different things, all vital. Whether you’re choosing your starting FPL team, or placing a bet on teams to win and players to score, the fixture difficulty rating is something you should focus on a lot more in the new season. What Fixture Difficulty Actually Measures The FPL Fixture Difficulty Rating assigns a score to each upcoming match based on opponent strength. At its simplest it tells you whether a player is facing a top four side or a team fighting relegation. But underneath that simplified number sits something much deeper, recent form, home and away performance splits, defensive and attacking matchup data, and how teams tend to set up against specific types of opposition. It’s a planning tool that needs to be utilised by more players. The managers who use it well aren’t just looking at next week. They’re looking three or four gameweeks ahead and making decisions now that pay off later. FPL Managers & Gamblers Should Think the Same That habit of forward planning based on fixture runs is exactly the kind of structured thinking that separates considered gamblers from reactive ones. FPL managers who spend time mapping out upcoming schedules before committing to transfers are doing something that most casual football punters never bother to do. This is looking at the context behind a match rather than just the names on the team sheet. The PFT Fixture Difficulty tool is one of the cleaner ways to visualise upcoming fixture runs across the whole Premier League, and it’s as useful for identifying betting angles as it is for planning transfers. For anyone already using that data to inform FPL decisions, applying it across UK betting sites to find value in match result or player markets is a natural next step. Where the Betting Market Gets Fixture Difficulty Wrong The market tends to price big clubs based on reputation rather than context. A top six side with a run of difficult away fixtures in the next three gameweeks will still be heavily favoured in each individual match, even when the cumulative picture suggests they’re likely to drop points. Equally, a mid table team with three consecutive home games against sides in poor form can be systematically underpriced week after week simply because casual fans back the bigger name. These are patterns that repeat across most seasons and show up when you look at the fixture picture in advance rather than on the morning of the game. Home and Away Differences Matter Analysis covering nearly 30 seasons of Premier League data shows that home teams win more frequently than away teams by a margin of 10-20 percentage points in nearly every season. This is a gap that has remained remarkably consistent over time, as documented in research from George Washington University’s data analysis programme That’s a significant edge, and yet betting lines don’t always fully account for it when combined with fixture context. How to Use Fixture Runs The most practical application is identifying teams with three or four soft fixtures in a row and backing them in cumulative markets. Every FPL manager builds their transfer strategy around these runs. A pplying the same logic to football betting markets means the research you’re already doing for your FPL team can be used twice over. The fixture is the same whether you’re picking a captain or placing a bet, the information just needs to translate across in a different way. articles.body: The Stats Behind Your FPL Captain Choice - Premier Fantasy Tools Last updated on August 19th, 2026 Ask any FPL manager where their season was won or lost and the answer is almost never a transfer, it’s the captain’s armband. A string of good captain picks over a full 38 gameweek season is worth hundreds of points and can be the difference between a top 10k finish and a frustrating mid table one. And yet for something so important, most managers treat it as an afterthought. Why the Captain Decision Defines Your Season The captain scores double points. That single mechanic means every gameweek has a moment of maximum leverage built into it. How well you use it generally has more impact than any individual transfer decisions you take. A player who returns 12 points gives you 24 as captain. A blank from your captain while a rival’s armband hauls in the points can cost you 20 places in a mini league overnight. Most managers can absorb a bad transfer here and there, but consistently poor captaincy is harder to come back from. The Safe Armband Option The most popular captain pick almost every gameweek is a premium asset with a decent fixture. The logic is sound, back your best player in a good game. The problem is what happens when 40-50% of managers do exactly the same thing. You can check exactly how concentrated ownership gets on the official Fantasy Premier League statistics page , the numbers are often more extreme than people realise. When the template captain blanks, everyone blanks together and the damage is shared. When they return, the gain is neutralised because your rivals got it too. This is where captaincy starts to look a lot like value betting. Following the obvious pick at short odds rarely builds a long term edge. Taking advantage of the best betting offers to find better odds across multiple platforms is the same instinct applied to football markets, the value is rarely where the crowd is pointing. In both cases, the question isn’t who’s most likely to score. It’s whether backing them at this price, or at this ownership level, actually gives you an edge. What Does the Data Say? Analysis of the top 50 FPL managers from the 2025/26 season found a captain success rate of around 23%. This is defined as picking the highest scoring player in your own squad as captain. Even the very best managers in the game get the optimal pick right less than a quarter of the time. The lesson isn’t that captaincy is a lottery. It’s that you’re making a probability decision every week. The goal is to make the highest expected value call, not to predict the exact outcome. The PFT Captain Picks Analyzer is one of the better tools for understanding your own captaincy patterns. This includes tracking your history, your success rate, and how your picks benchmark against the top managers in the game. Most people have no idea what their actual captaincy record looks like until they check. When to Take the Risk? Going against the template with the armband is a decision that should be deliberate, not reactive. The situations that justify it are specific. This includes things such as you’re behind in a mini league and need ground quickly, the favourite pick has a fixture that looks worse than the ownership level suggests, or there’s a player in genuinely elite form against a weak defence that others may have missed. Done right, a different captain call to the crowd can move you twenty places in a mini league in a single gameweek. Done wrong, it costs you the same. It’s risk and reward, and it’s this kind of decision making that makes FPL the game we all love. articles.body: From FPL To Away Days: How Premier League Fixtures Shape Football Travel - Premier Fantasy Tools Last updated on August 25th, 2026 Fantasy Premier League managers already read the fixture list like a map. A run of home matches, a difficult away trip, or a changed kickoff time can alter an FPL decision. For travelling supporters, the same calendar shapes flights, trains, hotels, and weekends away. NuxGame’s iGaming software sits in the wider digital sports ecosystem where live schedules, locations, and changing events matter, but the travel lesson starts with the Premier League calendar itself. The Fixture List Is Also A Travel Calendar For supporters planning an away day, the opponent is only part of the decision. Kickoff time can determine whether a same-day train is realistic, whether a hotel is needed, and how much of the destination can be explored before or after the match. Premier League fixtures can also move because of broadcasting, cup competitions, or other scheduling changes. That makes flexibility valuable. Booking the cheapest non-refundable journey immediately may save money, but it also creates risk when a match moves. The better travel plan leaves room for the football calendar to change. FPL Can Make Unfamiliar Cities More Interesting Fantasy football changes how supporters notice clubs outside their own team. Owning a player can make an otherwise neutral fixture more interesting, while a strong run of fixtures can put a club on an FPL manager’s radar for several weeks. That can influence travel too. A supporter may become curious about a stadium, neighborhood, or city because they have followed several players there throughout the season. Fantasy football turns the league into a broader network of places rather than a schedule centered on one club. Before turning an FPL fixture into a trip, it helps to check: Whether the kickoff time is confirmed Official ticket availability and restrictions Last practical train after the match Distance between stadium and accommodation Local transport on matchday What else the city offers nearby Matchday Travel Is Increasingly A Digital Experience A football trip now depends on more than a printed ticket and a timetable. Mobile tickets, train apps, mapping services, fixture alerts, live team news, and FPL updates can all be part of the same day. The physical journey is supported by a constant flow of digital information. That creates the same basic challenge seen across complex online platforms: information must stay current. NuxGame’s iGaming software operates in a different part of digital entertainment, but the underlying principle is familiar. When schedules, locations, account states, or live events change, outdated information can quickly become more frustrating than having less information in the first place. Global Football Audiences Still Travel Through Local Rules The Premier League has an international audience, but attending a match brings supporters back into a very local environment. Transport systems, ticket policies, venue rules, payment methods, and entry requirements depend on the place being visited. Global interest does not remove local conditions. The same distinction appears across other international digital industries. Businesses researching topics such as licensing in Anjouan are also dealing with the difference between global online reach and jurisdiction-specific rules. The subject is different, but the broader lesson is similar: digital access can cross borders easily, while rules and practical conditions remain attached to real places. The Match Should Not Be The Only Destination Some of the best football trips work because the match gives structure to a wider weekend rather than consuming every hour. An early arrival can leave time for local food, neighborhoods, museums, waterfronts, or simply seeing how football fits into the city beyond the stadium. FPL can make that kind of travel more varied. Following different clubs and players throughout a season creates reasons to look beyond the most obvious destinations. A fixture becomes the starting point, while the city provides the rest of the experience. The Premier League calendar therefore works as more than a list of matches. For FPL managers and travelling supporters, it can become a practical travel-planning tool: one that connects football interest with new cities, routes, and weekends away. The strongest plans treat the fixture as the anchor, but leave enough flexibility for both the schedule and the destination to surprise you. articles.body: FISO FPL Fixture Difficulty Planner 2026/27 – Plan Your Opening Gameweeks - FISO FPL Fixture Difficulty Planner 2026/27 – Plan Your Opening Gameweeks - Skip to content The 2026/27 Fantasy Premier League season is almost here, and with the new Premier League fixtures confirmed, FPL managers can start planning their opening squads whether it be for FPL or FanTeam’s £65k fantasy game Fixture difficulty is always an important part of pre-season planning. A player might look attractive in isolation, but a difficult opening run can considerably reduce his appeal. Conversely, identifying clubs with several favourable fixtures can help managers find defenders with clean-sheet potential, attacking players capable of producing early returns and useful lower-priced options. To help with that process, two months ago in June, FISO launched its new interactive Fixture Difficulty Planner (FDR) covering the opening ten Gameweeks of the 2026/27 Premier League season. Try the FISO Fixture Difficulty Planner: https://www.fiso.co.uk/games/fdr/ The Premier League season begins on Friday 21 August with Arsenal hosting promoted Coventry City and runs through to the final round on Sunday 30 May 2027. What is Fixture Difficulty Rating? Fixture Difficulty Rating – usually shortened to FDR – provides a quick visual indication of how difficult a team’s forthcoming fixtures are likely to be. The official FPL system rates fixtures from one to five, with one representing the easiest fixtures and five the hardest. The Premier League says its FDR uses formulas incorporating Opta data together with teams’ recent home and away form. FDR can be particularly useful when looking beyond an individual Gameweek. For example, an FPL manager deciding between two similarly priced defenders might discover that one has a significantly better run over the next five matches. Likewise, a run of favourable fixtures could strengthen the case for doubling up on a particular team’s defence or investing in one of their attackers. The FISO tool takes that idea further by allowing managers to create their own assessment of team strength. Why FISO’s FDR is different There is an obvious problem with any fixed Fixture Difficulty Rating: football supporters don’t necessarily agree about how strong every team is. A club rated as a difficult opponent at the beginning of the season could lose key players, suffer injuries or simply perform below expectations. Another team might make several strong signings and prove considerably better than initially expected. The FISO Fixture Difficulty Planner therefore makes team Strength editable. The initial ratings are based on performances from the 2025/26 season, but they are only intended as a sensible starting point. If you think a team is stronger or weaker than the default rating, simply change its Strength figure. The complete FDR immediately recalculates. That means you aren’t restricted to somebody else’s opinion of fixture difficulty – you can create your own. Home advantage is included – and adjustable Playing Arsenal at the Emirates shouldn’t have exactly the same difficulty as playing Arsenal at home. The FISO model therefore incorporates home advantage into its calculations. The default Home Advantage setting is 2, but this is also adjustable. Managers who believe home advantage should have a greater influence can increase it. Those who think the difference is relatively small can reduce it. Again, the entire fixture grid recalculates automatically. Nine colour bands make fixture runs easy to spot Rather than relying on only a few difficulty categories, the FISO FDR uses additional colour shades to provide greater separation between fixtures. At a glance, managers can identify: favourable fixture runs in shades of green; relatively neutral fixtures through the middle of the scale; increasingly difficult matches moving through orange and red. Each fixture also displays its underlying difficulty figure, providing more information than colour alone. The result is particularly useful when scanning several Gameweeks simultaneously. Compare the next 3, 5 or 10 Gameweeks One easy fixture isn’t necessarily a good reason to buy an FPL player. What happens afterwards is often more important. The FISO planner therefore calculates rolling difficulty figures for: Avg 3 – the opening three Gameweeks Avg 5 – the opening five Gameweeks Avg 10 – the entire period covered by the planner This makes it much easier to distinguish between a team with one attractive match and a club embarking upon a genuinely favourable run. The Premier League itself recommends looking at fixture difficulty over a period rather than concentrating solely on an individual match, and its pre-season analysis has highlighted the value of planning across the opening four-to-six Gameweeks. Sort the table to find the best fixture runs The FISO FDR isn’t simply a static fixture chart. Managers can sort the teams according to different periods, making it possible to identify the clubs with the strongest schedules for the part of the season that matters to their own FPL strategy. That could be particularly useful when building a Gameweek 1 squad. You might, for example, prioritise the first three Gameweeks if you’re expecting an aggressive early Wildcard, while another manager intending to hold their initial squad for longer may be much more interested in the five or ten-Gameweek ratings. Save and share your own FDR One of the most useful features is the ability to share your customised rankings. After changing the Strength ratings to reflect your own view of the Premier League teams, the planner can generate a shareable version. That makes it possible to post your FDR on the FISO FPL Forum and compare it with other managers. Think Manchester United should be rated higher? Think one of the promoted clubs is being underestimated? Adjust the numbers, see what happens to the fixtures and share your version with other FPL managers. Which teams have attractive early fixtures? The official Premier League FDR has already identified Manchester City and Manchester United among the teams with favourable schedules over the opening six Gameweeks. Manchester City’s early schedule, for example, contains home matches against Bournemouth, Coventry and Sunderland in the first five Gameweeks, along with a trip to Crystal Palace. The official FPL analysis gives City an average FDR of 2.8 over GW1–5. Arsenal, meanwhile, start the season at home to promoted Coventry before facing Aston Villa away and Chelsea at home. Their first six also include Sunderland, Brighton and Leeds. But that’s where the editable FISO ratings become useful. Do you consider Coventry significantly weaker than the rest of the Premier League? Increase the gap. Do you think another club’s summer recruitment makes them much stronger than their 2025/26 finishing position suggests? Increase their Strength. The fixture colours and rolling averages change accordingly. Why only GW1–10? The FISO tool deliberately concentrates on the opening ten Gameweeks. The main purpose is to help FPL managers with their pre-season squad selection and early-season planning. There is also little point pretending that the fixture calendar will remain untouched throughout the campaign. Television selections, domestic cups and European competitions can all affect scheduling as the season develops. Restricting the planner to GW1–10 therefore keeps the tool focused on the period when it should be most useful: selecting that initial 15-man squad and planning the first few transfers of the new season. Start planning your 2026/27 FPL squad Fixtures shouldn’t be the only factor when selecting an FPL player. Price, expected minutes, attacking potential, clean-sheet prospects, set pieces and individual form all matter. But favourable fixtures can make a good FPL asset considerably more attractive. The new FISO Fixture Difficulty Planner provides a quick way of finding those opportunities – while allowing you to decide for yourself just how strong each Premier League team really is. Use the FISO FPL Fixture Difficulty Planner: https://www.fiso.co.uk/games/fdr/ And if you want to discuss your ratings, opening squad or 2026/27 FPL strategy with other managers, head over to the FISO FPL Forum We use cookies to ensure that we give you the best experience on our website. Our Ad Partners may also use technology to customise ads shown to you. If you continue to use this site we will assume that you are happy with it.

articles.body: New Betting Sites for FPL Managers This Season - Premier Fantasy Tools Last updated on August 17th, 2026 Fantasy Premier League has always sat close to real football betting, and this season the overlap feels tighter than ever. Managers tracking a striker’s minutes for a captaincy pick are the same people who notice when that striker is priced as odds-on to score in the next fixture. The habits of studying form, checking injury news, and weighing up fixture difficulty translate almost directly from fantasy team selection to placing a bet, which is why so many FPL players end up browsing bookmaker offers during the same scroll session where they’re mulling a transfer. This crossover has coincided with a wave of new bookmakers entering the UK market, each trying to win over football-obsessed customers with sign-up offers, sharper odds, or features built specifically around the Premier League calendar. For anyone who spends their Friday evenings agonising over whether to bench a rotation risk, knowing which of these new sites are worth a look can save both time and money. Below is a rundown of some of the newer UK bookmakers making noise this season, along with where you can find a wider comparison of everything currently launching. Where to Track the Newest UK Bookmakers Keeping up with every new betting site that launches in a given month is genuinely difficult, since operators come and go, rebrand, or quietly pull out of the market within a year of arriving. For FPL managers who want a reliable way to see what has actually launched and stayed active, the newest UK bookmakers page on Compare.bet is a useful starting point, listing recently licensed operators alongside their welcome offers and core features. It saves the trouble of searching through forum threads or outdated blog posts that reference sites which no longer operate. The reason a dedicated tracking page matters is that the UK Gambling Commission licenses new operators fairly regularly, but not all of them are aimed at the same audience. Some target casino players first and treat sports betting as an afterthought, while others build their entire platform around football markets, live streaming, and same-game accumulators. Filtering out the ones that actually matter to a football fan takes some digging, and having a curated list cuts that process down considerably. Newer entrants also tend to compete hardest on introductory offers, since they need to draw customers away from long-established brands. That competition benefits the customer directly, particularly around big Premier League weekends when a new site might run enhanced odds or free bet promotions to build its user base quickly. Watching which new sites are gaining traction, rather than betting with the same operator out of habit, can genuinely improve value over a season. BetAhoy and Its Approach to New Customers BetAhoy is one of the more recently licensed operators to make an impression in the UK betting scene, and it has positioned itself with a straightforward welcome offer aimed at new customers rather than a complicated tiered bonus structure. This simplicity tends to appeal to bettors who have been put off by other operators’ bonuses that come loaded with wagering requirements and expiry dates that are easy to miss. The platform has also focused on covering domestic football thoroughly, which matters to FPL managers who want to place bets on the same matches they are tracking for fantasy purposes. Having a clean, uncluttered market list for Premier League fixtures makes it easier to find anytime scorer odds or clean sheet markets without wading through unrelated sports first. talkSPORT BET and the Media Crossover Model talkSPORT BET took a different route into the market by leaning on the existing talkSPORT radio brand, which already has a loyal football-following audience. Rather than building recognition from scratch, it borrowed trust from a media outlet that many bettors already listen to for match previews and pundit opinion. That familiarity has helped it gain traction faster than some fully independent new brands. Its markets are geared heavily toward the Premier League , with detailed player prop bets that overlap neatly with fantasy football decisions, such as odds on a player registering an assist or getting booked. For FPL managers deciding between two midfielders for a transfer, seeing how the betting market rates their attacking threat can be a useful secondary data point alongside the usual underlying stats. Midnite’s Focus on Younger, Mobile-First Bettors Midnite arrived with a clear target audience: younger bettors who do everything on their phone and expect a slicker, app-first experience rather than a desktop-first site with a mobile version bolted on. The interface strips away a lot of the visual clutter that older bookmaker sites carry over from years of incremental updates, which makes navigating to specific Premier League markets noticeably quicker. The site has also built out player-specific betting markets that closely mirror the kind of decisions FPL managers already make each week, including goal involvement markets and card-count props. That alignment between what fantasy managers are already analysing and what the site lets them bet on is a deliberate design choice, and it has helped Midnite carve out a niche among a football audience that skews younger than the customer base of more traditional bookmakers. Smaller New Entrants Worth Watching Beyond the more established newcomers, a handful of smaller operators such as Betsuna and Lad Bet have entered the UK market this year, typically with narrower feature sets but competitive introductory pricing. These sites often lack the polish or market depth of bigger new entrants, but they can still be worth a look purely for welcome offer value, especially for bettors who plan to shop around for the best odds on a single weekend of fixtures rather than sticking with one operator long-term. Which New Sites Actually Suit FPL Managers Best Not every new bookmaker is equally useful to someone thinking in fantasy football terms. The sites that tend to work best for FPL managers are the ones offering detailed player prop markets, since these mirror the exact decisions being made in a fantasy squad each gameweek, such as whether a forward is likely to score or a defender is likely to keep a clean sheet. Midnite and talkSPORT BET both lean into this kind of market depth, which makes them particularly relevant for anyone already immersed in stats-driven team selection. At the same time, simplicity has its own value. BetAhoy’s more straightforward offer structure suits managers who want to place the odd bet without needing to study terms and conditions closely. Ultimately, the right choice depends on whether someone wants deep, prop-heavy markets to cross-reference with fantasy decisions, or a simpler platform for occasional, low-effort bets on the same fixtures they are already following for FPL purposes. Making Sense of a Crowded New Market The number of new UK betting sites launching each year makes it easy to either miss genuinely good options or waste time on operators that add little beyond a flashy welcome page. For FPL managers, the practical approach is to treat new bookmakers the way they treat new signings in fantasy football: check the underlying detail before committing, compare what is actually on offer against established alternatives, and be willing to switch if a newer site proves better suited to weekly habits. With a reliable way to track new launches and a clear sense of which features matter for football-focused betting, sorting the useful new sites from the forgettable ones becomes a much quicker task. articles.body: When Should You Play Your First Half Chips in FPL 26/27? - Full90 FPL Skip to content When Should You Play Your First Half Chips in FPL 26/27? In this piece, we will be looking at how to use our first half chips in 26/27 Fantasy Premier League (FPL). If you don’t know what chips are, check out our FPL explained section. Right, let’s get into it! Two Schools of Thought – Planners & The Others There are two basic schools of thought to chips in FPL. We have the managers who like to plan out their chips and then we have the other guys. I sit firmly in the planning category. Whilst I think you can do perfectly well without a plan, I think it requires a bit of luck and/or a certain skill to know when the right moment to play your chips is that most of us don’t possess. With a plan, I can identify the moments ahead of time, make picks that make the most of those moments and I can always adjust plans as I go along. Wildcard There are two key factors of when to wildcard for me. Firstly, information . At the start of the season we have the least amount of information available to us. We haven’t seen the new managers, new signings and new tactics. So, the biggest information jump is from gameweek 0 to gameweek 1 – we get a huge amount of new information from that. In gameweek 2 we get a tonne of new information but it’s less than gameweek 1; gameweek 3 we get more new information but it’s less than gameweek 2. And so the trend goes on. So, we will probably want to and probably should wildcard early to fix our mistaken thinking. But, we also need enough information to make this wildcard worth doing. The second factor is fixtures. Naturally in FPL, you want to pick players with good fixtures. A wildcard allows you to rapidly switch to a bunch of guys with good fixtures. Most of the time, teams fixtures either get better or worse in different gameweeks. But some weeks there are more teams than others and we call these ‘big fixture swings.’ Those weeks are: Gameweek 4 – Chelsea, Arsenal, Newcastle, Palace and Everton have a good run of fixtures. Gameweek 6 – Arsenal, Bournemouth, Fulham all have good runs. Of course, you could also just use your wildcard when you’re in a bit of trouble with injuries and the like. But, realistically, I don’t think it’s likely that you end up with five injuries in your fifteen. And, with the ability to save up to five free transfers in FPL, it is even less likely that you will need a wildcard to save you. Triple Captain Triple Captain is actually one of the easiest to figure out. Just pick the best players in the game against the worst opposition in the league. And, to make it easier for you I have identified those gameweeks: Haaland v.s. Bruno v.s. Coventry (H) Hull (A) Ipswich (H) Ipswich (H) Hull (H) Coventry (H) The best fixture is probably Haaland at home to Hull. At the moment and until proven otherwise, Hull are the worst team in the league and Haaland has the highest ceiling of any pick in the game. However, waiting to gameweek 16 comes with risk. Haaland might not be fit at that point and there is no other obvious pick as all Bruno’s games have been played. He may also simply be rotated in an easy fixture against weak opposition following a couple of intensive months and just before the intense Christmas period. So, I think a less risky and still excellent pick is Haaland at home to Coventry in gameweek 3. It’s at home, there isn’t any European football either side so his minutes should be reassured and we know he scores more goals earlier in the season. Of course, there is nothing to stop you playing your triple captain on anyone else in the league. Someone like Palmer Saka could have excellent gameweeks but this carries a bit more risk as they tend not to hit the heights of Bruno or Haaland. Free Hit Free hit is also a relatively simple one. Pick a week when you have no players playing against a rubbish team or pick a week when your best players play against each other or both! If you have lots of Chelsea or Arsenal assets in your gameweek 1 team, you could free hit them out in favour of Man City players in gameweek 3 against Coventry (though obviously you cannot triple captain too!) and Liverpool players against Ipswich. Alternatively, if you have lots of Man United or Man City players in your gameweek 1 team, you could switch them to Chelsea assets in gameweek 4 when they play Hull. Bench Boost Bench boost is probably the most complex out of all these chips. It’s a bit frustrating in that regard because all we are talking about is adding the scores of 4 picks you don’t want in your first eleven most weeks. The best thing to do with a bench boost is to play it early. That means you can fill your bench with reasonably good picks when you are free to make as many transfers as possible. And then wildcard out of it reasonably early because you will probably have left a million or two in cash on your bench that you could use in your starting eleven instead. James’ Aggressive Chip Strategy Okay, I have set out the general view on chip strategy coming into the season. But here is my current plan: Bench Boost Gameweek 2 I want to triple up on Coventry at home against Hull. This helps me keep the bench cheap AND gives a great opportunity for points. Triple Captain Gameweek 3 – Haaland (H) v.s Coventry As explained above, he’s at home and fit and it’s early season. Free Hit Gameweek 4 Remove United and City, triple up on Chelsea v.s Hull I plan to go into the season with no Chelsea players. I don’t really think any of them are that great in the first couple of weeks so I want to bet against that opposition but bet big on them for the game against Hull. I can also have triple Palace against Ipswich, double Brighton against Coventry and Double Arsenal away to Sunderland as well as drop my double Man United defence against Man City. Wildcard gameweek 6 To take advantage of fixture swings and increased information. One of the important things about this plan is that the free hit and wildcard are not set in stone. If I think that the teams with fixture swings in 4 look much better than I expect then I will be able to simply wildcard then and free hit later (or in 3 to triple up on Liverpool). I’d rather give myself two more weeks of information before committing to a wildcard though. This strategy allows me to aggressively target fixtures against bottom opposition – principally Ipswich, Hull and Coventry. Assuming this goes well, and that is what I expect, then I will start the season with a good rank in the top 500k and not feel any need to chase success which I also really like. That’s It. Think strategically about how to use your chips and let me know if I have missed anything! This gameweek, that debate feels sharper than usual. Squad structures are being pulled apart and rebuilt in real time as managers weigh ownership trends against price-value ratios. The tension isn’t new, but the numbers behind it are worth examining closely. With early-season price changes already influencing decisions, managers are scrutinising every asset for signs of over- or under-ownership before committing their transfers. Community Sentiment On Budget Defender Options Budget defenders remain a hot topic in FISO threads this week, with many managers hunting for enablers who won’t drain funds needed elsewhere. The conversation often circles back to goalkeeper and defensive pairings that free up cash for premium forwards or midfielders further up the pitch. Names like Dubravka, Verbruggen and Van Ewijk keep appearing in squad-building discussions precisely because they offer solid starting minutes without eating into the budget. This isn’t just anecdotal chatter — the data backs it up. Recent ownership figures show Haaland sitting at 73.7% while cheaper forward options like João Pedro and Dominic Calvert-Lewin sit at 55.7% and 25.0% respectively. That pattern suggests managers are pairing one premium anchor with cheaper value picks rather than spreading spend evenly across the pitch. Premium Midfielders Facing Rotation Risk Concerns Midfield selection is where the real headaches begin. Rotation risk is a constant worry for anyone backing an expensive attacking midfielder, and this gameweek’s discussions are no exception. Managers are asking whether locking in a premium name is worth it if minutes aren’t guaranteed every week. Between debating transfers, plenty of FISO members also chat about how they spend their downtime away from the pitch data. Streaming documentaries about football tactics fill evenings between matchdays. Fantasy sports apps keep engagement high during international breaks. Podcast deep-dives on transfer windows and manager decisions pass the time on commutes. Some browse fixture previews and others check odds boards. A fair few explore gambling options, as the best paying UK casinos by GamblingInsider ,with clearly listed payout rates and structured operator comparisons, offer a straightforward starting point for anyone curious about that corner of the entertainment world. Off-Pitch Fan Engagement And Side Games Beyond transfers and captaincy calls, the FISO community thrives on side games and prediction leagues that run alongside the main FPL competition. These mini-games keep engagement high even in weeks where the main squad doesn’t need much tinkering. They also give managers a lighter, more social way to test their football knowledge against friends. One player whose rise illustrates how quickly consensus can shift is Antoine Semenyo, who moved to 56.0% ownership after being among the most-bought assets in six consecutive gameweeks last season, according to Premier League statistics . That kind of surge shows how fast a mid-priced player can become a template pick once returns start flowing. Weighing Differential Picks For Rank Climbers For managers chasing rank rather than protecting a lead, differentials remain the most tempting — and riskiest — route. The appeal is obvious: a lower-owned player who delivers can swing thousands of places in a single gameweek. The risk is equally obvious when that same player blanks. Bryan Mbeumo’s ownership climbed 7.1 percentage points to 23.8% recently, the biggest midfield rise in the latest snapshot, showing how quickly sentiment shifts once form and fixtures align. Anyone comparing last season’s returns against current prices might find the recent breakdown of best value FPL assets useful for spotting where the market may be undervaluing certain players. Ultimately, the differential debate comes down to appetite for risk versus reward — and this gameweek, that calculation feels finely balanced across the FISO community. articles.body: FPL Price Change Predictor 2026/27: Live Guide The official FPL Price Change Predictor is now live for 2026/27. Log in to Fantasy Premier League and select Price Changes to see which players are moving towards a price rise or fall. The predictor uses official FPL transfer activity and updates every 15 minutes. It is a timing guide rather than a guarantee, so use it alongside minutes, fixtures and team news before making a transfer. The feature was launched by the Premier League after the Gameweek 1 deadline . For other squad-building data, visit our free FPL tools , including the FPL DEFCON comparison tool What is the official FPL Price Change Predictor? The predictor is an official Fantasy Premier League page that tracks every player's progress towards the next price rise or drop. It shows current progress as a percentage calculated from official transfer activity. After a calibration period of at least one Gameweek, FPL says it will also show a predicted progress percentage. Labels such as “Very Likely to Rise” and “Likely to Drop” translate the data into a quicker status. This is the first official FPL tool dedicated to predicting price changes. Third-party services have estimated changes for years, but they have had to infer the unpublished thresholds from player ownership and observed changes. Is the FPL Price Change Predictor live? Yes. The predictor became available after the Gameweek 1 deadline on 21 August 2026. To find it: log in on the Fantasy Premier League website select Price Changes in the main navigation; and filter the table by your team, your watchlist or all players. Player prices were locked before the Gameweek 1 deadline. They can now rise or fall at the daily price-change update. What does the predictor show? The main table lists every player and can be filtered to show: players in your team; players on your watchlist; or the full player pool. Price-change status also appears on individual player profiles. FPL says the Pick Team and Transfers screens will include a price-change view, letting managers check their own squad as part of the normal transfer workflow. What does a percentage over 100 mean? According to the Premier League, anything above 100 per cent indicates that the player is expected to pass the rise or fall threshold at the next 00:00 UK update. It still does not guarantee a change. For example, a player could display 105 per cent shortly before midnight, then receive enough late transfers in the opposite direction to move back below the estimated threshold. FPL explicitly describes the predictor as a guide. Treat the status as evidence for timing a move, not a promise that the price will change. How often is the FPL predictor updated? The predictor page updates every 15 minutes. Player price changes happen once per day at 00:00 UK time The percentage can move in either direction as managers continue buying and selling players. A stale screenshot or an update from earlier in the day may no longer represent the current position. The most important limitation remains the same: predicted progress is not the only factor in a good transfer. Should you make an early transfer to avoid a price rise? Sometimes, but price protection has a cost. An early transfer can secure a player before a rise and preserve team value. It also exposes your squad to injuries, rotation news and other information that arrives before the next deadline. Before moving early, consider: whether the player is likely to start; whether either club has another match before the FPL deadline; how much the possible price change affects your planned move; whether you would still want the player at the higher price; and whether you have a free transfer or would take a points hit. A predicted rise can make the timing urgent, but it does not make the underlying transfer good. Decide on the player first, then use the predictor to decide whether waiting is worth the risk. Official predictor versus third-party price-change sites The official tool has one major advantage: it is built from official FPL transfer data and integrated into the game. That does not necessarily make every independent tool redundant. Third-party services can still differentiate through: notifications before a likely change; historical prediction accuracy; daily price-change histories; combined transfer, fixture and expected-points analysis; and alternative views for planning several moves. FPL has also said its own prediction remains a guide. The value of any predictor should be judged by how clearly it communicates uncertainty and how accurately it performs after calibration. When do FPL prices change? FPL price changes happen at 00:00 UK time Official FPL price-change rules say a player can rise or fall by £0.1m in one daily update and by up to £0.3m in a Gameweek. The predictor's percentage is designed to show who is approaching the next change. Check it close enough to the update to use current information, but do not let a possible £0.1m move override a better transfer decision. Our FPL defensive contribution guide explains another new-season factor to consider when comparing players. If your group would rather draft unique squads and trade players during the season, Draft Fantasy for the Premier League supports auction and snake drafts, waivers, trades and custom scoring. Read the 2026/27 launch guide for the full setup. Create a 2026/27 Premier League Draft Fantasy league FPL Price Change Predictor: quick answers Where is the FPL Price Change Predictor? Log in to the Fantasy Premier League website and select Price Changes in the main navigation. Does 100 per cent guarantee a price change? No. It indicates that a player is expected to pass the threshold, but transfers can move the percentage before the midnight update. How frequently does the predictor update? The predictor page updates every 15 minutes. Player prices change at 00:00 UK time. How much can an FPL player's price change? A player can rise or fall by £0.1m per day and by up to £0.3m in one Gameweek. Want a fantasy game where players move between managers through waivers and trades instead? articles.body: Fantasy Football Waiver Wire: Gameweek 3 Pickups Anthony Elanga is the best Gameweek 3 waiver claim. Lewis Hall is the priority defender, while Eddie Nketiah is the forward to add before his points catch up with his chances. Pascal Groß offers a safer midfield role; Dan Ndoye and Amar Dedić are deeper-league alternatives. This is advice for draft leagues , where each player has one owner. The roster rate measures how often a player is already owned across completed private Draft Fantasy leagues, so first check who is actually free in your Draft Fantasy Premier League transfer market. Scoring note: the order uses Draft Fantasy regular scoring, which matches official FPL scoring. Custom-scoring leagues calculate points from the commissioner's values, so extra rewards for shots, chances created or defensive actions can change the order. The Gameweek 3 claim order Best fantasy football waiver claims for Gameweek 3 Priority Player Pos Rostered GW1–2 GW3–5 Anthony Elanga NEW Midfielder 39.1% 17 pts · 156 min BOU LEE HUL Lewis Hall NEW Defender 47.2% 14 pts · 180 min BOU LEE HUL Pascal Groß BHA Midfielder 32.4% 15 pts · 180 min LEE COV ARS Eddie Nketiah CRY Forward 7.7% 3 pts · 122 min FUL IPS LEE Dan Ndoye NFO Midfielder 4.7% 12 pts · 126 min TOT AVL COV Amar Dedić NEW Defender 8.7% 12 pts · 180 min BOU LEE HUL Draft Fantasy regular-scoring totals and private-league roster rates, 1 September 2026; fixture difficulty runs from 1 (easiest) to 5 (hardest). All ten Gameweek 2 matches had finished on the pitch when this snapshot was taken, but the official post-Gameweek review had not locked the round. Small scoring corrections remain possible. The ranking is built on roles, underlying involvement, roster availability and three fixtures rather than one provisional bonus point. Create a Premier League draft league to play with unique squads, configurable waivers and a live transfer market. Why Elanga leads the order Elanga has started both matches, scored in both and played 156 minutes. The two goals came from 0.42 expected goals, so the finishing rate will not continue unchanged. His role is still more useful than the headline: he registered three shots on target and Newcastle's run improves from Bournemouth at home to Leeds away and Hull at home. A 39.1% roster rate makes him available often enough to justify an aggressive claim. Use 8–14% of remaining FAAB as an editorial starting range when he would enter your lineup. Spend less when he would only replace bench depth; these are bid guides, not fixed player prices. Hall is the defender to claim; Dedić is the fallback Hall has completed 180 minutes and followed an 11-action defensive game in Gameweek 1 with 13 defensive contributions, a clean sheet and maximum bonus in Gameweek 2. His 0.66 expected assists across two matches also gives him an attacking route that does not depend on another clean sheet. The concern is availability rather than evidence: Hall is already rostered in 47.2% of completed private leagues. Start around 7–12% of remaining FAAB if he is free and upgrades a weekly starter. Dedić is the practical second request. He has also played every minute, then added an assist and two key passes in Gameweek 2. His 8.7% roster rate makes him far likelier to survive to a fallback claim. Bid 1–4% , because Hall owns the stronger creative numbers even though both receive the same fixture run. Groß supplies the safer midfield role Groß has two full matches, six key passes and 0.38 expected assists. A goal and an assist at Chelsea produced the Gameweek 2 return, but the 90-minute role and chance creation are the reasons to buy. Leeds at home and Coventry away are rated two and one before a much harder Arsenal fixture. Rank him above a volatile scorer when you need a midfielder to start immediately. An editorial range of 6–10% of remaining FAAB is reasonable; custom leagues that reward key passes can move him closer to Elanga. Brighton teammate Diego Gómez is the lower-cost alternative. He has two assists, 0.56 expected goals and 0.65 expected assists in 175 minutes, but using both midfielders as separate high bids would overcommit to the same fixtures. Put Gómez behind Groß in the same request chain instead. Nketiah is the forward whose process beats his points Nketiah has only three points, which is why he remains rostered in 7.7% of leagues. The underlying case is much better: two starts produced 0.96 expected goals, 0.58 expected assists and three key passes in 122 minutes. He now faces three opponents rated two, one and two. This is not a guarantee that the finishing changes in Gameweek 3. It is a chance to buy a scarce starting forward before a return makes him obvious. Use 4–8% of remaining FAAB when he replaces a forward without secure minutes. Managers with three dependable forwards should preserve their budget. Ndoye is the deeper-league upside claim Ndoye has started twice but played only 126 minutes, so his role is less secure than those above him. Gameweek 2 supplied the upside: a goal, two key passes, 0.35 expected goals and 0.63 expected assists in 65 minutes. Nottingham Forest also receive difficulty ratings of one, three and one over the next three. Treat him as a fifth-midfielder claim, not proof that a six-point average will last. A 1–4% bid is enough in most FAAB leagues. If you need a steadier 90-minute floor, Groß should remain higher in the queue. Hold last week's hits, but step back from Emersonn The strongest Gameweek 2 waiver recommendations mostly reinforced their roles. Mamadou Sangaré, Anton Stach and Keane Lewis-Potter each played at least 87 minutes; Sangaré and Stach again reached double figures for defensive contributions, while Lewis-Potter added an assist. Do not drop them merely because their second score was lower than the opening return. Maxim De Cuyper also played 90 minutes and now reaches the favourable Leeds and Coventry fixtures. Thierno Barry failed to score but generated 1.48 expected goals in 69 minutes, then moves into two difficulty-one fixtures after Manchester United. Both remain holds. Emersonn is the exception. He fell from 65 minutes to 45, produced no shot and is now flagged with a knee problem in the official player data. Do not add him before his availability and role are clearer. That is new evidence, not a verdict on the opening goal. Build a claim queue around the player you will drop Fix a weak starter before adding depth. Elanga, Hall or Groß should lead when one immediately improves your lineup. Pair alternatives in one position. Use Hall then Dedić at defender, or Groß then Gómez at midfield, rather than six unrelated requests. Pay for role and opportunity. Nketiah's three points can be more actionable than a bench player's isolated goal. Protect scarce FAAB and priority. The fantasy football waiver rules guide explains how bidding, rolling priority and weekly reset change the cost of each claim. Check the full run. The free fixture difficulty tool shows why a neutral Gameweek 3 matchup can still lead into two strong starts. The verified Gameweek 3 deadline is Friday 4 September at 17:30 UTC . Waivers follow the processing schedule shown inside your own league, so submit the queue before that process rather than waiting for the match deadline. Ready for a transfer market where every decision matters? Start a Draft Fantasy Premier League league , invite your managers and choose FAAB, rolling or weekly-reset waivers.

articles.body: Why Am I Missing a Free Transfer in FPL? | OneFPL Loading OneFPL page In this article sections The short answer If you think FPL has not given you a free transfer, the most common reason is that you used a Wildcard or Free Hit in the previous Gameweek. The free transfer received for the chip Gameweek is used as part of activating that chip. Previously banked transfers are not lost. Example You enter GW5 with: two saved free transfers; plus the normal new Gameweek transfer. You play Free Hit. The new GW5 transfer is used by the chip. Your two previously saved transfers remain available in GW6. What about Triple Captain or Bench Boost? Those chips do not use your weekly transfer. If you played Triple Captain or Bench Boost and made no transfer, the normal free-transfer rules continue. Other reasons the number may look wrong Check whether: you already used a free transfer; you were already at the maximum bank of five; you activated Wildcard or Free Hit; you are looking before the next Gameweek transfer has been awarded. Maximum bank You can store up to five free transfers If you already have five, leaving another transfer unused will not create a sixth. Read How many free transfers can you bank in FPL? OneFPL verdict Before assuming there is an account problem, check your previous Gameweek's chip and transfer history. The official FPL Transfers page shows your full history. articles.source_type: Season tips, pre-season club lessons, chip strategy, captaincy calls
articles.body: What Happens If Your FPL Captain Does Not Play? | OneFPL Loading OneFPL page In this article sections The short answer If your FPL captain records zero minutes , the captain multiplier moves to your selected vice-captain. If the captain makes any official appearance, even a short cameo, the multiplier stays with the captain. Captain and vice-captain outcomes Captain Vice-captain Result Plays Any outcome Captain scores x2 0 minutes Plays Vice-captain scores x2 0 minutes 0 minutes Nobody receives x2 Late cameo Plays Captain keeps x2 What happens with Triple Captain? The same promotion rule applies, but the multiplier is Triple Captain Vice-captain Result Plays Any Captain scores x3 0 minutes Plays Vice-captain scores x3 0 minutes 0 minutes Triple bonus is lost The chip is not returned if neither player plays. Does a one-minute cameo keep the captaincy? Yes. An official appearance means the captain keeps the multiplier. That is why expected minutes matter when choosing a captain or Triple Captain. Are automatic substitutions different? Yes. Auto-subs decide which bench player replaces a zero-minute starter. The captain multiplier moves only to the selected vice-captain — not to the substitute entering the XI. Can Triple Captain be cancelled before the deadline? Yes. Triple Captain can be cancelled before the Gameweek deadline. Read FPL Triple Captain explained OneFPL tools Use OneFPL Team News before the deadline and the Live Table during the Gameweek. articles.body: Can You Undo an FPL Transfer? Current 2026/27 Rules | OneFPL Loading OneFPL page In this article sections The short answer A confirmed normal FPL transfer cannot be reversed. However, chip cancellation rules are different. What can and cannot be cancelled? Action Can it be cancelled? Confirmed normal transfer ❌ No Triple Captain ✅ Before deadline Bench Boost ✅ Before deadline Free Hit after confirmation ❌ No Wildcard while still Pending ✅ In limited cases Active Wildcard ❌ No Captain / vice-captain / bench changes ✅ Before deadline The current Wildcard Pending rule The official 2026/27 FAQ adds an important detail. If the Wildcard still shows as Pending with zero or one confirmed transfer, it can still be cancelled. Once a second transfer is confirmed, the Wildcard becomes Active and cannot be reversed. Can Wildcard remove a transfer hit? Yes. Transfers already made in the same Gameweek become free when the Wildcard becomes active. This can remove a -4, -8 or larger transfer deduction from that Gameweek. Can a Free Hit be cancelled? Not after the Free Hit transfers have been confirmed. Can Triple Captain or Bench Boost be cancelled? Yes , before the Gameweek deadline. Avoid transfer mistakes Before confirming: test the move in the OneFPL Transfer Planner check Team News; confirm the points cost; check your remaining free transfers; then make the official transfer. FAQ Can I undo a confirmed transfer? No. Can Wildcard remove a -4? Yes, if the Wildcard becomes active in that same Gameweek. Can I cancel Triple Captain? Yes, before the deadline. Can I cancel Bench Boost? Yes, before the deadline. Can I cancel Free Hit? No after confirmation. articles.body: How to Get a List of All Team IDs in Your FPL Mini-League — FPL Ranker Loading FPL Data... Fetching the latest information from Fantasy Premier League Blog ← Back Blog tips · cover TIPS How to Get a List of All Team IDs in Your FPL Mini-League FPL Ranker August 13, 2026 What an FPL team ID is Every Fantasy Premier League squad has a permanent numeric team ID, sometimes called an entry ID or manager ID. It appears in the URL of any manager's team page: fantasy.premierleague.com/entry/1234567/event/1 — the 1234567 is the team ID. The ID is public. It is how the official Fantasy site links to a squad, and it is what third-party tools ask for when they load someone's team. It is not a password and it grants nobody access to your account — knowing your ID lets someone view the same public squad page that the official league table already links to. The manual method: one ID at a time Open your mini-league on the official Fantasy Premier League site, go to the Standings tab, and click a manager's team name. That opens their squad page, and the number in the URL after /entry/ is their team ID. Copy it, go back, and repeat for the next manager. This works, but the official standings page never shows the IDs as a list — so a 20-manager league means 20 round trips through the URL bar, and there is no export. That is the whole reason this question gets asked. The fast method: the Ambassador tab Each ID links straight to that manager's official Fantasy squad page, and Export CSV downloads the whole roster — rank, team, manager, team ID, total points, gameweek points, the official FPL link and an FPL Ranker link for each manager. Copy list puts the same roster on your clipboard for a group chat. It is sign-in gated on purpose. A roster of manager names and IDs should not be bulk-scrapeable by anyone who happens to know a league code, so exporting is tied to a real account. 1. Open the Ambassador tab on your league. 2. Export CSV pulls every team ID into one file. (IDs are blurred in this screenshot; yours show in full.) What to do with the list The common use is comparison. With every ID in one place you can pull up any rival's squad, see their captain, and check their transfers without hunting through the official table each week. The export opens straight in Google Sheets, Excel or Numbers. Every row is one manager — rank, team name, manager name, FPL team ID, total points, gameweek points, a link to their official Fantasy squad and a link to their FPL Ranker page — so you can sort it, filter it, or paste a single column into whatever tool you use next. The other use is the one the tab is named after. Share the CSV in your league chat so everyone can paste their own ID into a tool and see their season — rank movement, gameweek headlines, and where they actually gained and lost ground. A mini-league is more fun when everyone can see the story, not just the table. The same export opened in Google Sheets — one row per manager, ready to sort, filter or share. Why does the official FPL site not show all the team IDs? How many managers can I export at once? Fetching the latest information from Fantasy Premier League Blog ← Back Blog STRATEGY Top 5 Fantasy Premier League Tools for 2026/27 (and How to Use Them) FPL Ranker July 26, 2026 The best Fantasy Premier League tools for 2026/27 each solve a different job: the official FPL site for the game itself, Fantasy Football Scout for Opta stats, LiveFPL for live rank and effective ownership, Fantasy Football Fix for fixture planning, and FPL Page for a live matchday dashboard. Understanding the newer scoring systems — BPS and defensive contributions (DEFCON) — and pairing a transfer planner with a mini-league tracker is what turns raw data into rank. What makes a great FPL tool in 2026/27 The best setup is not one site — it is a stack. You want live rank and effective ownership on matchday, Opta-grade underlying stats for transfer decisions, a fixture planner for the medium term, and a mini-league tracker for the bragging rights. Two scoring systems now shape picks. The Bonus Point System (BPS) decides the 1–3 bonus points per match from a blend of on-ball actions, while defensive contributions (DEFCON) reward defenders and midfielders for tackles, interceptions and blocks — making busy ball-winners viable budget picks. A transfer planner ties it together: mapping two or three gameweeks ahead against fixtures and predicted price changes is how you avoid wasted hits. How this list works (and why we link out) This is an honest, tool-by-tool comparison — we link straight to each site so you can try them. We rebuild this list regularly with a fresh angle as tools ship new features. No tool does everything, so we have noted the single job each one is best at, plus where FPL Ranker fits into the stack. The top 5 FPL tools for 2026/27 Ranked by how essential each is to a complete workflow — official game first, then the specialists. Official Fantasy Premier League The game itself, plus the official Scout picks, price changes and the definitive player prices and status flags. Your source of truth before any third-party tool. Fantasy Football Scout Opta-powered stats, predicted line-ups and a large community, with a season ticker and projections behind membership. Best for deep, data-led transfer decisions. LiveFPL The gold standard for live rank estimation and effective ownership during matches, plus chip-impact analysis. Best for tracking exactly where you stand on matchday. Fantasy Football Fix Opta statistics, a fixture planner and an AI-assisted team optimiser. Best for medium-term planning and stat-sandbox exploration. FPL Page A clean live dashboard covering live rank, bonus, defensive contributions, price changes, xG/xA and effective ownership in one view. Best for an at-a-glance matchday cockpit. FAQ What is the best FPL tool for 2026/27? There is no single best — it is a stack. Use the official FPL site for prices and status, Fantasy Football Scout or Fantasy Football Fix for Opta stats and planning, LiveFPL for live rank and effective ownership, and FPL Page for a matchday dashboard.
